newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook-output may weigh on gasoline.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook-output may weigh on gasoline.

text.p: Strong U.S. refinery operations, together with expectations for a steady flow of imports, could put some pressure on Gulf and New York Harbor gasoline prices in the coming week, market analysts said on Tuesday.
"I don't think this brief run-up is going to sustainable," said Ken Miller, senior principal at the Houston consultancy Purvin and Gurtz.
Indeed, gasoline prices started the week on a bearish track, with the June NYMEX shedding about 3.80 cents before finding support and rebounding.
NYMEX prices had moved higher in the run-up to the three-day Memorial Day weekend, with spot NYMEX gasoline futures reaching two-month highs on Friday.

Cash spot gasoline prices also firmed modestly last week in anticipation of Memorial Day, the traditional start of the summer "driving season," traders said, helped by last week's American Petroleum Institute report which showed stocks nearly seven million barrels below previous year levels.
Prompt conventional M1 gasoline at the U.S. Gulf jumped from a bottom at about 56.50 cents early in May to about 65.25 cents by the end of last week.

"The market typically in the second quarter peaks in (refinery) margins and in gasoline prices," Miller added. After that, the market is very vulnerable to oversupply over the course of the summer as refineries boost output, he added.

Strength in refining margins means the downstream producers are likely to keep their operations near maximum capacity for the near term, market players said. The API put refinery operations at 97.6 percent of capacity in its latest report.

In addition, the restart of Tosco's Trainer, Pennsylvania refinery should added more than 100,000 barrels a day of gasoline to the East Coast markets. That refinery, which was shut by BP prior to its sale to Tosco in January 1996, is expected to be at full capacity by the end of the month.

In the Midcontinent, delays on the Explorer Pipeline system will continue to be a factor in the market this week, although traders said they expect demand to begin to recede, keeping prices largely steady.
"I don't see a whole lot of upward pressure in this market," said a Houston-based trader. "It appears most people who needed to cover their requirements did so."
Midco gasoline differentials to the NYMEX jumped at least four cents recently on the combination of pipeline delays and refinery snags.
In addition, supply along the Williams system has begun to increase in the Group Three markets due to the slight step down in demand.

Traders pegged supply at 19 days, a two day increase from last week. Prices of unleaded gasoline, however, still remain strong, with values currently at about 5.00 cents over the screen. The average price in May last year was 2.20 under NYMEX July.
